section.title: Overcoming the World
section.sectionRationale: As the letter closes, John binds faith, love, and obedience together and shows that faith in Jesus as the Son of God is the God given victory over the world. He then marshals the witnesses God has provided, the Spirit, the water, and the blood, and God's own testimony, all converging on the Son in whom eternal life is found.
section.thesis: Everyone born of God overcomes the world through faith in Jesus the Son of God, and this faith rests not on feeling but on the testimony God has given about His Son, whose sum is that God has granted us eternal life, and this life is in the Son alone.
section.frameNote: Three beats: faith in the Son as the victory that overcomes the world; the threefold testimony of the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and God's greater testimony, that eternal life is given in His Son.

verses.text: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been {{gennao|born of God}}, and everyone who loves the Father also loves those born of Him.
By this we know that we love the children of God: when we love God and keep His commandments.
For this is the love of God, that we keep His commandments. And His commandments are not burdensome,
because everyone born of God {{nikao|overcomes}} the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world: our {{pistis|faith}}.
Who then overcomes the {{kosmos|world}}? Only he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God.

units.label: The threefold testimony
units.note: the Spirit, the water, and the blood

verses.text: This is the One who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ, not by water alone, but by water and blood. And it is the Spirit who testifies to this, because the Spirit is the truth.
For there are three that testify:
the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and these three are in agreement.

units.label: God's testimony about His Son
units.note: eternal life is in the Son

verses.text: Even if we accept human testimony, the testimony of God is greater. For this is the {{martyria|testimony}} that God has given about His Son.

Whoever believes in the Son of God has this testimony within him; whoever does not believe God has made Him out to be a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has given about His Son.
And this is that testimony: God has given us {{zoe|eternal life}}, and this life is in His Son.
Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.

gennao.gloss: To beget, to give birth; in the passive, to be born. This is John's word for the new birth: everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God. This divine begetting, not human effort, is the source of faith, of love for God and His children, and of the power to overcome the world.

nikao.gloss: To conquer, overcome, prevail, be victorious. The one born of God overcomes the world, and the decisive victory has already been won. It is the same word Revelation uses for the overcomer; here the conquest is not by force but by faith joined to the Son who has Himself overcome the world.

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust, belief; reliance on God and on His testimony about His Son. This is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith. Faith is not a work that earns the victory but the empty hand that lays hold of the victorious Christ, resting on what God has said and done.

kosmos.gloss: The world; here the created order in its organised rebellion against God, the realm that lies under the power of the evil one. To overcome the world is not to escape it but to refuse its allegiance and its lies, holding fast to Christ who has conquered it.

martyria.gloss: Testimony, witness, evidence given. John stacks up witnesses to the Son: the Spirit, the water, and the blood, and above all the testimony of God Himself. Faith rests on this reliable testimony that God has given about His Son, and the believer carries that testimony within.

zoe.gloss: Life, and especially eternal life, the very life of God shared with His people. This life is not merely endless existence but life in the Son: whoever has the Son has life. It is God's own gift, given now and secured forever in Christ.

basic.context: John is drawing his letter to a close by tying its threads together. To believe that Jesus is the Christ is to be born of God, and those born of God love the Father and His children and keep His commands, which are not a heavy burden. Why not? Because everyone born of God overcomes the world, and the victory that overcomes it is our faith. Then John points to the witnesses that make faith reasonable: Jesus came by water and blood, the Spirit testifies, and God Himself testifies about His Son. The bottom line is simple: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son. Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son does not have life.
basic.hermeneutics: This passage is often misread as if faith were a burst of willpower that conquers our troubles, or as if the water and the blood were riddles. John's point is steadier. Faith overcomes the world because it unites us to the Son who has already overcome it. The water and the blood recall how Jesus came, through His baptism and His atoning death, real events that God, the Spirit, and history attest. Assurance is not wishful thinking; it rests on God's own testimony about His Son.
basic.originalLanguages: Everyone born of God, gennao, overcomes, nikao, the world, kosmos, and the victory is our faith, pistis. God stacks up witnesses, and the key word is testimony, martyria, given supremely by God about His Son. The sum of that testimony is life, zoe, eternal life, which is found in the Son alone.
basic.typology: The threefold witness echoes the law's requirement that a matter be established by two or three witnesses; here the Spirit, the water, and the blood confirm the Son. The water and the blood also recall the cleansing and the sacrifice of the old covenant, both fulfilled in Jesus, who came by water and blood.
basic.christ: Everything centres on the Son. To believe that Jesus is the Christ and the Son of God is to be born of God and to overcome the world. He is the One who came by water and blood, attested by the Spirit. And He is the place where eternal life is found: whoever has the Son has life. There is no life in general on offer, only life in Him.
basic.god: God is the chief witness. He has not left faith to guess; He has given testimony about His Son, and to refuse it is to call God a liar. This God gives eternal life as a gift, not a wage, and He secures that life in His Son so that those who believe may hold it with confidence.
basic.crossReferences: John 16:33 says Jesus has overcome the world. John 19:34 records water and blood flowing from His pierced side. John 5 speaks of the Father's testimony about the Son. And John 20:31 states the purpose of belief: that believing, you may have life in His name.
basic.oneStory: The whole Bible calls for witnesses to the truth and points to the One in whom life is found. Here the witnesses converge on Jesus: the Spirit, the water, the blood, and God Himself. The long search for life, lost in Eden, ends in the Son, for God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son.

context.literary:
This section is the hinge between the second great movement of the letter and its closing. John has twice circled the tests of life, righteousness and love, and here he draws them together by naming their common root, new birth, and then their common ground, the testimony of God. The words 'born of God' open the unit in verse 1, return in verse 4 and recur in 5:18, so the passage and the verses beyond it are bound by that phrase.

Look at how the argument chains. Believing that Jesus is the Christ gives birth, birth gives love, love gives obedience, obedience is light because birth gives victory, and victory is faith. Each step is announced by the little word 'for' or 'because', the grammar of an argument in which every link leans on the one before. Verses 1 to 5 move in a circle that starts and ends with belief in Jesus: verse 1 says believing in the Christ, and verse 5 says believing that Jesus is the Son of God.

The second half turns from the people who believe to the One they believe in, and the vocabulary changes accordingly. The key word becomes testimony, used again and again in verses 6 to 11, together with its verb. John is arguing as a lawyer would, setting out his witnesses and then moving to the verdict. The structure is a small trial scene. The case is stated in verse 6, the witnesses are called in verses 7 and 8, the rule of evidence is invoked in verse 9, the consequences for accepting or rejecting the evidence are given in verse 10, and the judgment is declared in verses 11 and 12.

The closing two verses are written in an almost poetic parallel: whoever has the Son has life, whoever does not have the Son does not have life. The words are tight and symmetrical, and the second line adds the full title 'the Son of God', which echoes the first line of the passage and closes the circle.
context.historical:
The vocabulary of victory was loaded in the first-century world. Nike was a goddess whose winged figure appeared on coins, monuments and public buildings across the Roman cities, and Rome presented its emperors as conquerors. In that setting a small and sometimes suspect community was told that its own victory was already won, and was won by faith. The claim would have sounded at once humble and astonishing. The world that John means is not the empire only but the whole order of human life organised without God, 2:15-17.

The witness language belongs to the courtroom and to the Law. A matter had to be established by two or three witnesses, Deuteronomy 19:15, and Jewish tradition took that principle very seriously. John's Gospel already spoke in these terms, with the Father, the works, the Scriptures, John the Baptist and the disciples all called as witnesses to Jesus, John 5:31-39 and 8:17-18. When the elder wrote that God's testimony was greater than any human testimony, his readers knew the rules of evidence being applied.

The 'water and blood' were a live matter for a church shaken by the departure of those who denied that Jesus Christ had really come. Irenaeus tells us of a teacher, Cerinthus, who held that a divine Christ came upon Jesus at his baptism and withdrew before his death. If that was the sort of teaching the seceders of 2:19 had adopted, a message that celebrated the baptism but quietly dropped the cross would have been attractive to those who found the suffering of God's Son an embarrassment. John answers that Jesus came by water and by blood, together.

The commandments that are 'not burdensome' also have a background. Some of the church's surrounding religious cultures, Jewish and pagan, knew heavy systems of rules and rituals. Jesus himself had spoken of the heavy loads placed on people and offered a light burden in their place, Matthew 11:28-30. John's readers had not been freed from obedience, but their obedience had a different engine. The letter is generally placed in the last decades of the first century.
context.canonical:
The language of birth from above runs through the New Testament. Jesus told Nicodemus that no one can enter the kingdom of God without being born of water and the Spirit, John 3:5-8, and the prologue of the Gospel said that those who receive him are children 'born not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God', John 1:12-13. Peter writes of a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus, 1 Peter 1:3. John's own letter has already said that anyone born of God refuses to practise sin, 3:9, and that everyone who does what is right has been born of him, 2:29.

The theme of victory has a long background. Israel's conquests, the crossing of the sea, and the fall of Jericho were attributed to faith by the writer of Hebrews, Hebrews 11:29-30. Jesus ties the thought to himself on the night before his death, 'take courage; I have overcome the world', John 16:33. In Revelation the Lion of the tribe of Judah 'has triumphed', Revelation 5:5, and the same word is used of believers who overcome through the blood of the Lamb, Revelation 12:11, and who are promised a share in his throne, Revelation 3:21. Paul says that in all our troubles we are more than conquerors through him who loved us, Romans 8:37.

The three witnesses are taken from the law's rule of evidence, Deuteronomy 19:15, and applied in the Gospels and by Paul, 2 Corinthians 13:1. The Spirit's testimony is promised in John 15:26 and echoed in Romans 8:16, where the Spirit testifies with our spirit that we are God's children.

Finally, 'life in the Son' gathers a theme running from the garden, where the tree of life stood, Genesis 2:9, to the final chapter of Revelation, where the tree is again beside the river of life, Revelation 22:2. The Gospel of John states the same purpose, 'that by believing you may have life in His name', John 20:31, and Jesus says plainly, 'I am the way and the truth and the life', John 14:6.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John writes to people who have been unsettled by departures and who need to know what they stand on. He therefore gives them a sequence that moves from the inside out. Inwardly they have been born of God. That birth shows in what they believe, in the love they bear, and in the willing obedience that follows. Outwardly the world will oppose them, but the opposition does not decide the outcome.

He also writes to remove a fear that obedience is a weight that will finally crush the believer. The statement that God's commands are 'not burdensome' is not a statement about easy rules but about the new nature that desires what God desires. Anyone who has been born of God has been given a new will, and the commands accord with it. John means his readers to read the commandments as a description of the life they already want.

Further, he intends to settle the ground of assurance in the testimony of God and not in changing moods. The long section on the three witnesses is not a puzzle for scholars. It is a practical gift: a believer lying awake with doubts can reflect that the evidence is not in the heart's fluctuating feelings but in what God has said about his Son. Refusing that evidence insults God, verse 10, and trusting it is to rest where God himself rests.

Finally, John's purpose in verses 11 and 12 is to reduce everything to a single sentence that a child could repeat and no clever teacher could improve. Life is a gift and is found in a person. He wants his readers to hold on to that sentence when the church is confused by sophisticated alternatives.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verses 1 to 5 contain both descriptions and implicit commands. 'Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God' describes what has happened to a believer. 'We keep His commandments' describes what the born-again do, and the passage does not issue an explicit instruction to try harder. It would be a mistake to read verse 4 as a command to 'overcome the world' through determination. It is a statement of what is true of those who have faith.

The statement that God's commands are 'not burdensome' is likewise a description. It is not meant to say that obedience is always felt as easy or that believers never struggle, as John's own earlier words about confession and cleansing, 1:8-2:2, show. It says that the commands do not oppress, because they flow from a heart that loves, and because God's grace is present to help.

The most delicate point is the closing statement of verse 12. It is stated as a fact, and the passage records the consequence for those who lack the Son. Application should be careful. It is a call to hold to Christ and to speak of him with urgency, not a licence for confident pronouncements on the eternal state of particular individuals. John writes to the community of believers to reassure them, and so the verse is best used for the same purpose today, as a ground of assurance for those who trust the Son and a clear, humble invitation for those who do not.

debates.question: What are 'the water and the blood' in verse 6?

views.label: Jesus' baptism and his death
views.case: This is the reading most often defended. John stresses 'not by water alone', which makes best sense if a teaching existed that honoured the baptism and set aside the cross. At the baptism the Father and the Spirit testified to the Son, Matthew 3:16-17, and at the cross the Son's blood was shed, Romans 3:25. The word 'came' in verse 6 refers to the whole public career of Jesus, which was framed by those two events.

views.label: The flow from the pierced side
views.case: John 19:34 records that blood and water came out when a soldier pierced his side, and the author calls attention to it as an eyewitness, John 19:35. Many early and later interpreters have read 1 John 5:6 in the light of that scene, with water as cleansing and blood as atonement. The order differs, though, and the verse speaks of how Jesus came, not only of one moment.

views.label: The sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper
views.case: Many in church history have found the sacraments pictured in water and blood. The idea is that they carry on the testimony to Christ in the church. The weakness is that the verse is about how Jesus came, in the past, and the opponents' error was about his person, not about the church's rites.

debates.bearing: All three readings make the same point where it counts: God's Son is attested by real events in the body of Jesus, not by a religious experience detached from history. Any reading that keeps both the baptism-type event and the death of Christ real guards what John wants guarded.

debates.question: Does new birth come before faith, or does faith come before new birth?

views.label: New birth is the cause of faith
views.case: The grammar of verse 1 puts a present tense, 'everyone who believes', with a perfect, 'has been born', so that the birth is a completed event with ongoing results and believing is its visible evidence. John 1:13 says believers were born 'not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God', and John 3:8 compares the Spirit's work to the wind. Many in the Reformed tradition read this as showing that God's new birth gives rise to faith.

views.label: Faith is the condition and new birth the result
views.case: Others point to John 1:12, where those who received and believed were given the right to become children of God, and to the passages that call for belief in order to have life, John 20:31. They read the perfect in verse 1 as a description of the state that follows believing, not a statement of cause.

views.label: The two are held together and not set in sequence
views.case: Some argue that John is not describing a time order at all. He treats belief, birth, love and obedience as aspects of one change, and sets out the marks so that a believer can know they are in it. Seeking to settle the order may press the verse for a question it was not written to answer.

debates.bearing: John's purpose is assurance: a person who believes and loves can be certain that something has happened in them that only God could do. Whichever way the order is settled, no part of the credit belongs to the believer, and faith is received as a gift, Ephesians 2:8-9.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 pairs two tenses with care. 'Everyone who believes' is a present participle, pisteuon, a continuing trust, and 'has been born' is a perfect, gegennetai, the lasting result of a birth. The grammar therefore treats ongoing faith as the visible sign of a birth that has already happened. The verb gennao looks both ways. It is the verb for a father's begetting and a mother's bearing, and John uses it in verse 1 so that the same word covers the Father who begets and the child begotten, as the BSB footnote shows. That is why love for the Father extends naturally to the other children.

Verse 3 says the commands are not 'burdensome'. The Greek word, barys, means heavy or weighty, and it is the opposite of what the false teachers' regime would have been to ordinary believers. Jesus used a different word in Matthew 11:30, where his burden is 'light', but the thought is the same: obedience to him is not a crushing weight.

Verse 4 has a small surprise. 'Everyone born of God' is in the neuter in the Greek, literally 'everything that has been born of God', and the phrase becomes collective, the whole new-born family. The verb 'overcomes' is in the present tense, nika, a continuing triumph. Then the noun nike, 'victory', appears. This is the only place in the New Testament where the noun occurs, though the verb is common in John and Revelation. And the phrase 'that has overcome the world' is an aorist participle (nikesasa), pointing to a decisive, completed act. The victory that overcame is a past event, and the faith that lays hold of it overcomes now. Verse 5 asks the question with a present participle, 'the one who overcomes', and answers with a confession.

The noun pistis, 'faith', is a rare word in John's writings. It appears nowhere in his Gospel and only here in his letters, where he normally uses the verb pisteuo. It is a surprising place for him to choose the noun, and it suggests a settled, standing posture of trust as well as an act. Its object is carefully specified in verse 5: Jesus as the Son of God.

The word kosmos in John carries several senses. It can mean the created order, John 1:10, the human race that God loves, John 3:16, and the system of human society organised against God, as here and in 2:15-17. Verse 4 is about the third sense, which is why 'overcome' is the right verb. The 'world' is a power that must be defeated.

Verse 6 says Jesus came 'by water and blood', with the preposition dia, 'through', and then repeats the phrase with en, 'in', in the second clause. The aorist participle elthon, 'having come', looks back at the whole sweep of his coming. The Spirit is the one 'testifying' (to martyroun), a present participle, and the verse says the Spirit is the truth.

In verses 7 and 8 the Greek has a notable irregularity. The participle for 'those who testify' is masculine plural, even though the three nouns, spirit, water and blood, are neuter. The masculine form lets the three speak as persons. Verse 8 ends 'and the three are in agreement', literally 'are into the one' (eis to hen eisin), which means they converge on a single point. The BSB follows the older Greek manuscripts. Later Latin and some late Greek copies added an expansion about the Father, the Word and the Spirit 'in heaven', which the BSB footnote records, and which is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts and from most modern translations.

Finally, martyria, 'testimony', and its verb martyreo are leading Johannine words, in the Gospel and the letters, and they belong to the language of the courtroom. In verse 10 the believer 'has the testimony in himself' and the unbeliever 'has made Him a liar', a perfect tense (pepoiiken), the lasting state that results from refusing God's word. Verse 11 says God 'has given' (aorist, edoken) eternal life, a single completed act, while verse 12 says 'whoever has the Son has life' in the present.

typology.type: The sprinkled water and blood of the old covenant
typology.fulfillment: When the covenant was sealed at Sinai, Moses took the blood of calves and goats, along with water, scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled the scroll and all the people, Hebrews 9:19-20. Cleansing and atonement belonged together under the law: water to wash away defilement and blood because 'the life of the flesh is in the blood', Leviticus 17:11. John says Jesus came by water and blood, and the escalation is that what the law's rites pictured is accomplished in a person, the blood of a better sacrifice, Hebrews 9:11-14. The type falls short because the old rites were repeated and could not clear the conscience, while Christ's offering was made once for all, Hebrews 10:10-14.

At God's command Moses struck the rock and water came out for the people to drink, Exodus 17:6. Paul says the spiritual rock that accompanied Israel was Christ, 1 Corinthians 10:4. The water that flowed from the struck rock is a picture of life given through one who is struck, and John 19:34 shows the water flowing from the pierced side, with the Gospel writer insisting he saw it, John 19:35. The correspondence is not a coded riddle in every detail, and the text does not claim it is. The escalation is that the one smitten is the Son himself, and the water given is eternal life, John 4:14. The type falls short in that Israel's water satisfied for a day.

The people passed through the Red Sea and the walls of Jericho fell 'by faith', Hebrews 11:29-30. God fought for them, and the weapon was trust in his promise. John's 'this is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith' lifts the pattern from a nation's battles to the believer's struggle with the world's whole pressure. The escalation in Christ is that the great enemy is no longer a king or a city but the world order and its ruler, who has been judged, John 12:31, and Christ's victory comes before ours, John 16:33. The type falls short because the early victories were temporary and fought in a particular land, whereas this victory is for every believer in every place.

The tree of life stood in the middle of the garden, and after the fall the way to it was barred, Genesis 3:22-24. Life was withheld from sinners. John says that this life is now given and that it is 'in His Son'. The correspondence is that life is not a possession we hold apart from God but a gift found at its source. In the last pages of Scripture the tree stands again beside the river, Revelation 22:2, and the Son who is the life brings his people to it. The type falls short, since the tree was a created thing and a place, while the life of John 5:26 is in the Son himself, who has life in himself as the Father does.

study.christ:
The section is built from one end to the other around the person of Jesus. He is called the Christ in verse 1, the Son of God in verses 5, 10, 12 and 13, and Jesus Christ in verse 6. John piles up the titles because the faith that overcomes is faith in the whole person and not in a part of him. The Christ is the promised king of Israel and the Son of God is the eternal Son, and the church confessed that these belong to the same person.

The 'water and blood' show how he came. At the Jordan, Matthew 3:16-17, the Father's voice and the descent of the Spirit declared him to be the beloved Son, and he took up the work of his ministry. At the cross his blood was shed for sinners and he 'bore our sins', 1 Peter 2:24. Those who wished to keep a Christ without a cross could accept the first and not the second. John will not allow it. The Gospel writer insisted on the sight of blood and water from his side, John 19:34-35, and the apostle's claim in the letter, 'This is the One who came by water and blood', is made on the strength of what had been seen. The Son did not merely appear to die.

He is also the one who has already conquered. In John 16:33 he says it before he goes to the cross, and in Revelation he is the Lion who 'has triumphed', Revelation 5:5, who overcame and sat down on his Father's throne, Revelation 3:21. Believers' faith overcomes the world because it grasps the one who has overcome it. He is both the source of victory and the form it takes: the lamb who conquers by being slain.

Verses 11 and 12 reach the center. 'This life is in His Son.' Christ does not merely teach about life or open a road to it. Jesus says, 'I am the resurrection and the life', John 11:25, and 'I am the way and the truth and the life', John 14:6. In 1:2, John had written that the eternal life which was with the Father 'was revealed to us', which identifies that life with the person the apostles saw. The Father has life in himself and has granted the Son to have life in himself, John 5:26. So to 'have the Son' is not to possess an object but to be joined to a person who is himself the life.

Notice also that the Spirit testifies to Christ, as in John 15:26, 'He will testify about Me'. The Spirit's whole ministry is aimed at the Son. And in verse 5 we are given the object of the overcoming faith as a person: it is not a theory of Christ, but 'Jesus is the Son of God'.

One point of caution: not every phrase in the passage is a hidden code. We need not hunt for a reference in every word. John tells us what he means. The links we have traced come from the New Testament's own testimony, and each rests on a passage that says what it says.
study.god:
Perhaps the most arresting thing in this passage is that God is a witness. The one who is the judge of all submits his word to the rules of evidence and lays out his case. He does not expect people to believe in a vacuum. He has given the Spirit's testimony, the testimony of the historical events of Jesus' coming, and, above them all, his own spoken testimony about his Son. The God of Scripture is not content to command; he persuades, and he does so by telling the truth.

Because he is a truthful witness, he cannot be a liar. John presses this to the limit in verse 10: not to believe God's testimony is to make God a liar. Paul speaks of 'God, who cannot lie', Titus 1:2, and Numbers 23:19 says that God does not lie, nor does he promise and fail to fulfil. To doubt the testimony about the Son is therefore not a harmless caution but a verdict on God's character. It also shows how much the believer's confidence is a statement about God and not about ourselves.

He is the God who gives life as a gift. 'God has given us eternal life', verse 11, uses the language of giving, the same word as Romans 6:23, 'the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord'. Life is not earned by keeping the commandments of verses 2 and 3, though those who have it do keep them. The order protects both grace and obedience. The commandments are the evidence of the life, not the price of it.

He is the sovereign Father of a family. Believers are 'born of God', which places the origin of the Christian life in his will and not in human achievement, John 1:13. That birth is not a vague spiritual experience but the beginning of a new family resemblance, so that love for the Father brings love for his other children. Throughout, the God of the passage works through three persons in agreement, the Father who testifies, the Son who came, and the Spirit who is the truth.

He also gives commands that do not crush. His law has always been meant for life. Deuteronomy 30:11 says the command is not too difficult, and Jesus says his yoke is easy and his burden light, Matthew 11:30. A God who commands and also supplies the will to obey is a God of grace even in his demands.

For worship, this passage invites a posture of trust. We praise him by believing what he has said, by taking him at his word about his Son, and by living in the victory that faith holds. To worship the God of verses 9 to 12 is to stop asking for more proof than the one he has already given, and to rest in the life he has placed in his Son.

crossReferences.note: Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one can enter the kingdom without being born of water and the Spirit and compares the Spirit's work to the wind. This shows the birth John speaks of is a gift of God's Spirit, beyond our control, and gives a background for 'born of God'.

Those who received Jesus and believed in his name were given the right to become children of God, born not by human desire or will but of God. The verse holds together faith and divine birth, the same pairing John sets out in 5:1.
On the night of his betrayal Jesus tells his disciples to take courage because he has overcome the world. It is the root of John's confidence in verse 4 and the reason faith can be called a victory.

The one who overcomes is promised a place on Christ's throne, just as he overcame and sat down with his Father. It shows that the believer's overcoming is a share in the victory of Christ and leads to reigning with him.

Jesus invites the weary to come to him, take his yoke and find rest, for his yoke is easy and his burden is light. This is the Gospel counterpart to John's statement that God's commands are not burdensome.

Two or three witnesses are required to establish a matter. John builds on this rule, and the passage shows that God not only meets the standard but exceeds it, with the Spirit, the water, the blood and his own testimony.

Jesus says that another testifies about him, and that the Father himself has testified, in addition to his works. The same list of witnesses is behind 1 John 5:9, and the 'greater testimony' is the Father's own.

When the soldier pierced his side, blood and water flowed out, and the one who saw it has testified to this so that you may believe. The beloved disciple's eyewitness claim is the background for the letter's stress on a Christ who really bled.
At Jesus' baptism the Spirit descended and the Father spoke from heaven, 'This is My beloved Son.' This is the likeliest meaning of 'water' in verse 6, a public attestation by God of who Jesus is.

Paul speaks of eternal life that God, who cannot lie, promised before time began. It supports John's argument that rejecting God's testimony makes him a liar, and shows that the gift of life rests on his truthfulness.

Jesus says he is the resurrection and the life and that whoever believes in him will live even though he dies. It is the Gospel statement behind 'this life is in His Son' and shows that life is a person to be trusted.

In all our troubles we are more than conquerors through the one who loved us. Paul's phrase fits John's statement that the world is overcome, since both locate the strength of the conqueror in Christ's love and not in our own power.

study.oneStory:
Humanity's first loss was the loss of life. In the garden the tree of life stood in the middle, God said that disobedience would bring death, and the couple were sent out so that they could not eat of the tree and live forever. From then on the story asks where life can be found. The patriarchs are buried, Israel wanders in a wilderness, and the Law, which promises life to those who keep it, is broken. The prophets speak of a day when God will pour out water, put his Spirit within his people and give them new hearts, as in Ezekiel 36:25-27, which mentions both water and Spirit.

John's passage claims that day has come. The new birth is the beginning of a new humanity: a people born of God and no longer of the will of the flesh. Their weapon against the world is faith, and their victory has a name, because the one in whom they believe has already overcome. The long war that began in Genesis 3, between the seed of the woman and the serpent, is going the way God said it would.

The witnesses sum up the covenant story. The law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter. The prophets bore witness, John the Baptist bore witness, and the Father bore witness at the Jordan. Now the Spirit, who spoke through the prophets, bears witness in the church, and the blood and water of the story's centre in Jerusalem stand as events that cannot be taken away. A faith that hangs on events has something to stand on. It is not wishful thinking but the answer to a trial in which the evidence is in.

The close of the passage fastens everything to one claim. Life is a gift, and it is found in the Son. The story's ending in Revelation draws all the threads in: the Lamb who has conquered, the river of the water of life, the tree of life with leaves for the healing of the nations, and those who overcome inheriting all things, Revelation 21:6-7 and 22:1-2. What was lost in the garden is given back with more. The people who believe in the Son have the first fruits of it now, and the whole new creation will have it when the world that has been overcome is finally remade.

sermon.title: Faith Is the Victory
sermon.why: Begg preaches this section, 1 John 5:1-5, showing that genuine faith in Jesus as the Son of God is the victory that overcomes the world and the ground of assurance. A clear, orthodox handling of the passage.

quiz.q: According to verse 4, what is the victory that overcomes the world?

options.text: Our faith, which lays hold of Christ who has already overcome the world.
options.note: The victory is Christ's, and faith is the hand that receives it.

options.text: Our steady moral effort against temptation.
options.note: The fruit is real, but the ground of victory is faith in the victorious Christ, not our striving.

options.text: A promise of worldly success and ease.
options.note: The world here is the realm in rebellion against God; the victory is holding to Christ against it.

options.text: Nothing; the world cannot be overcome.
options.note: John says the opposite: everyone born of God overcomes the world.

quiz.q: What does John mean that Jesus came 'by water and blood' (verse 6)?

options.text: By His baptism and His atoning death, both real and attested by the Spirit.
options.note: John stresses not water alone but water and blood, against those who denied that the Son truly suffered.

options.text: By the water and blood that flowed from His pierced side.
options.note: A true echo of John 19:34, but John speaks of how Jesus came, spanning His baptism and His death.

options.text: By the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper.
options.note: The framing points to events in Jesus' own coming, not to later church ordinances.

options.text: By a symbolic Christ who never truly suffered.
options.note: This is the very error John writes to refute.

quiz.q: Whose testimony does John say is greatest?

options.text: God's own testimony about His Son.
options.note: The testimony of God is greater, and faith rests on it.

options.text: The witness of reliable human teachers.
options.note: John accepts human testimony but says the testimony of God is greater still.

options.text: The believer's inner feelings.
options.note: Feelings rise and fall; John grounds assurance in God's testimony, though believers do carry it within.

options.text: No testimony can be trusted.
options.note: John says God's testimony is sure, and to reject it is to call God a liar.

quiz.q: How does John describe eternal life in verses 11 and 12?

options.text: As God's gift, located in His Son, so that to have the Son is to have life.
options.note: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son.

options.text: As God's gift that we then keep by our own faithfulness.
options.note: Life is a gift secured in the Son, not maintained by our performance.

options.text: As a reward earned by obedience.
options.note: John calls it a gift God has given, not a wage we earn.

options.text: As something every person already possesses.
options.note: John says whoever does not have the Son does not have life.

options.text: Because those born of God overcome the world, and love makes His commands the glad response of a new heart.
options.note: New birth and love, not grudging duty, make obedience light.

options.text: Because with practice and discipline obedience grows easier over time.
options.note: Growth is real, but John roots this in the new birth and love, not mere self-discipline.

options.text: Because God has relaxed what He requires of believers.
options.note: God has not lowered His commands; He has given a new heart that loves to keep them.

options.text: Because keeping the commands is what earns our new birth.
options.note: John reverses the order: new birth comes first, and obedience flows from it.

questions: John says the victory over the world is our faith in Christ, not our willpower. Where are you trying to overcome sin or temptation by effort alone, rather than by trusting the Son who has already overcome?
Faith rests on the testimony God has given about His Son, not on our shifting feelings. When your assurance wavers, where do you look first, and how might God's own witness steady you?
John says whoever has the Son has life, and whoever does not have the Son does not have life. How does this sharpen the way you think about people who are religious but not resting in Christ?
God's commandments are not burdensome to those born of God. Which of God's commands still feels like a burden to you, and what would change if love, not duty, drove your obedience?
To be born of God shows itself in loving God's children. Whose face comes to mind as the test of whether that new birth is real in you?

translationNotes.note: 'By water and blood' most likely refers to Jesus' baptism and His atoning death, against teachers who denied that the divine Son truly suffered; the phrase 'not by water alone, but by water and blood' presses that both are real.

A later addition, often called the Johannine Comma, expands these verses in some manuscripts to read 'the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one' before 'the Spirit, the water, and the blood'. It stands in the Textus Receptus behind the King James Version but is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts, so the BSB rightly places it only in a footnote. The doctrine of the Trinity does not depend on it and is taught clearly elsewhere in Scripture.
The BSB renders the clause 'this is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith'; the original marks faith as the decisive means of a victory already won in Christ.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for 1 John 5:1-12. the wording is otherwise unchanged. The Johannine Comma at 5:7-8, absent from the earliest manuscripts and present only as a BSB footnote, is handled in the translation notes.
